doc.title: Frank Tate interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001

title: Joe Venuti: working with him and the legends about him
summary: Tate recalls Venuti relaxed at The Columns, difficult when ill, and doubts the famous Venuti stories.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: Well I found out something afterwards that really changed my opinion of him. When he came to The Columns and worked with Dave and Kenny Hawkins on drums and I was playing bass, he was very relaxed and very at ease and had a great time and swung like mad and was taking everybody to dinner, was the toast of the Cape and you know he was really having a ball. Because with Dave and the trio he didn’t have to think about a thing. He’d call a tune and Dave was in there even if we weren’t. And Dave was solid as the Rock of Gibraltar and Joe loved coming up there. And then when I worked with him with a different band he was kind of a load, he was kind of hard to handle. And it turned out he was very ill and I didn’t know it. And only one or two people knew about it. He subsequently died and he was a difficult person. But he was always an unrefined load of gold or whatever, I don’t know what I’m looking for here. He was basically I don’t think he had much formal education. He had a lot of musical education. He was a very fine violinist and when he was very young was I think he considered a symphony career. But I was very fond of him despite it all. I was crazy about him. And he was quite ill and none of us knew it.
Yeah. Quite a practical joker, wasn’t he?

Uh, I didn’t see that. But I mean I heard all the stories. But you know that story about all the bass players on the corner? Well I heard him tell it to some New York people that it took place on Hollywood and Vine and I heard him tell it to some California people and it took place at 52nd and Broadway, and I’ve never met anybody who met anybody who knew anybody who knew anybody that was involved. I really question the whole thing. And then there’s another story, we don’t even have to go into that, you know the one I’m talking about, I’ll pass on that. But I don’t know it seems like I guess it’s in the Sudhalter book on Bix, the story of Whiteman firing Venuti and Whiteman, it was somehow after a concert and he led the band — the orchestra — with a lighted baton and Venuti was to
follow him and he found a two by four and put some oily rags on it and lit him on fire and led the band. Again, I don’t know anybody that ever saw any of this stuff happen.
Right. What’s myth and what’s reality?
